topic.title: The offer letter and the rent receipt
topic.claim: Your CTC is a number you brag about, but the real salary is whatever is left after the landlord, and in big cities that is a much smaller number.
topic.behaviour: We compare offers by the monthly figure and the designation, then find out in the first week that the flat near the office eats most of it. By the third week we are counting every rupee and calling it 'the price of the city'.
topic.mechanism: Companies compete on the number that fits in an offer letter, while the biggest cost sits outside it, in a rent market no HR team controls. The landlord collects the raise the recruiter announced.
topic.group: Salaried people aged 24 to 32 moving to Mumbai, Delhi NCR or Bengaluru for a first or second job
topic.moment: You accept the offer, open a property app that night, and the happy feeling drops a little with every listing.

turn.believed: A bigger salary means a better life in a bigger city.
turn.actually: Past a point, a raise only changes who you pay it to. The city takes it first, and you get the leftover.

topic.feeling: cheated by a number that looked like progress
topic.villain: a rent market that prices housing off the salaries companies announce
topic.because: Landlords price rents against what young professionals in the area earn, so every salary hike gets priced into the next rent. Employers still sell the offer as the number, since that is the part they control.

proof.fact: Knight Frank data for H1 2026 shows Mumbai Metropolitan Region and NCR above 50% of household income going to home-loan EMIs.

topic.payoff: Before you say yes to any offer, subtract the rent of a flat you would actually live in. Whatever is left is the real offer.
topic.send_to: The friend who just got an offer in Mumbai or Gurgaon and is only talking about the hike.
real_details: An HR head said, 'For Gen Z and millennials, the offer letter now has to be read alongside the rent receipt.'
topic.news_peg: Report on young professionals weighing job offers against housing costs, 2026-10-21, with Knight Frank H1 2026 data on EMI share of income
topic.why_now: Offer season, Diwali bonuses and new-year job switches are all coming, and the rent question decides every one of them.

sources.fact: HR heads say candidates now compare job offers on what is left after rent and travel. Knight Frank's H1 2026 data puts MMR and NCR above the 50% EMI-to-income mark and the other six of the eight largest markets below it.
sources.excerpt: the offer letter didn't show what Mumbai would actually cost me. | candidates now compare offers on the money left after rent and travel. | A salary is only as good as what's left after rent, deposit and commute. | Knight Frank India's Affordability Index tracks the share of household income that goes towards home loan EMIs.

sources.fact: Knight Frank's H1 2026 index shows MMR homebuyers need about 69% of household income for EMIs, and MMR and NCR are the only two of the eight largest markets above the 50% threshold. This measures home-loan EMIs, not rent, so it supports the claim only indirectly. The 69% figure also looks inconsistent with the roughly 47–48% reported for Mumbai in earlier Knight Frank releases, so check it against Knight Frank's own report.
sources.excerpt: Homebuyers need about 69% of household income for monthly loan payments, unchanged from 2025. | significantly better than the 77% recorded in 2016 and 2019. | the most financially stretched housing market among India's eight largest cities. | An EMI-to-income ratio above 50% is generally considered unaffordable. | the only two markets where affordability exceeds the benchmark threshold of 50%.

cover.headline: Your CTC is for bragging. [Your landlord] decides your salary.
cover.sub: The hike in your offer letter already has a second owner.

paragraphs: Your CTC is for bragging. Your landlord decides your salary.
Swipe to read →
slides.why_swipe: How does the landlord get a say in my salary?

paragraphs: You accept the offer and tell home "a huge hike". That night you open a property app.
A 1BHK near the office in Powai wants around ₹40,000. Then a deposit of a few months' rent. The happy feeling drops a little with every listing.
HR controls the number in the offer letter. The city sends its bill later.
slides.why_swipe: So how much of the raise actually survives?

paragraphs: Say you jump from ₹12 lakh in Pune to ₹18 lakh in Mumbai. Your in-hand goes up by roughly ₹35,000 a month.
Your rent goes from ₹15,000 to ₹40,000.
You got the raise. Your landlord got most of it.
slides.why_swipe: Is that just bad luck, or is it built that way?

paragraphs: It's built that way. A flat isn't priced by its walls. It's priced by who rents nearby: people holding offer letters like yours.
That's why the broker asks "Which company?" before the budget. And the 11-month agreement brings every round of hikes to your door at renewal.
slides.why_swipe: Can't you just buy instead and stop feeding the landlord?

paragraphs: Buying only swaps the landlord for a bank.
On home loans, Knight Frank's H1 2026 data puts EMIs in Mumbai and NCR above half of household income.
And an EMI is a rent you can't walk out of.
slides.why_swipe: So is everyone on the same salary paying the same price?

paragraphs: And the same CTC is two different salaries. HR puts you and a colleague who lives with his parents in the same band, with the same appraisal.
He goes home to the family flat. Yours loses ₹40,000 to the city before it reaches you.
slides.why_swipe: So what does this do to how you live after the move?

paragraphs: By the third week you're counting every Swiggy order and calling it "Bombay ka kharcha".
That isn't you being bad with money. The money left in the first week.
We call it "the price of the city" so it doesn't sound like a pay cut. It was one.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you find the real number before you sign?

paragraphs: The real test runs on monthly in-hand, not CTC. Take each offer's in-hand. Subtract the rent of a flat you'd actually live in near that office. Compare what's left.
Sometimes the smaller offer wins. The bigger CTC still wins the family WhatsApp group.

end.save: Open this again the night an offer letter lands in your inbox.
end.send: Send to the friend who just got a Mumbai or Gurgaon offer and only talks about the hike.
end.promise: How money really moves in India.

draft.caption: What was your hike when you moved cities, and how much of it went straight to rent?
draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post. It argues that your CTC is the number you brag about, while your real salary is what is left after rent in a big city like Mumbai. It opens on the night you accept an offer and browse a property app, with ₹40,000 rents for a 1BHK in Powai and a deposit of a few months' rent, as the happy feeling drops with every listing. It walks through a move from ₹12 lakh in Pune to ₹18 lakh in Mumbai that adds about ₹35,000 a month in hand while rent jumps from ₹15,000 to ₹40,000. It explains that flats are priced by who rents nearby, which is why brokers ask which company you work for, and that the 11-month agreement brings every round of hikes to your rent at renewal. It notes that buying only swaps the landlord for a bank, since Knight Frank's data shows home-loan EMIs in Mumbai and NCR take over half of household income. It points out that two colleagues on the same CTC take home different salaries if one lives with his parents, and that we call the loss 'the price of the city' when it was really a pay cut. It ends with a test: compare offers on monthly in-hand minus the rent of a flat you would actually live in, because sometimes the smaller offer wins, though the bigger CTC still wins the family WhatsApp group.

claims.text: On home loans, Knight Frank's H1 2026 data puts EMIs in Mumbai and NCR above half of household income.
A jump from ₹12 lakh in Pune to ₹18 lakh in Mumbai CTC adds roughly ₹35,000 a month in hand (typical example).
claims.derived_from: ₹6 lakh CTC increase × about 70% after tax and deductions ≈ ₹4.2 lakh a year ÷ 12 ≈ ₹35,000 a month

claims.text: Rent going from ₹15,000 to ₹40,000 takes ₹25,000 of the ₹35,000 monthly raise, which is most of it (typical example).
